questions.question: What is the first step in a systematic step-by-step blood relation solver?
options: Guess the final answer directly
Parse each statement into individual direct relations before attempting to combine any of them
Skip statements that seem irrelevant
Assume the family has exactly four members
questions.rationale: A systematic solver first parses every statement into its individual direct relations before attempting any composition, avoiding premature or incorrect combinations.

questions.question: What does 'generation distance' measure between two people in a family graph?
options: The number of years between their birthdays
The number of parent-child links separating them in the family graph
The physical distance between their homes
Whether they share the same first letter in their name
questions.rationale: Generation distance counts how many parent-child links separate two people in the graph — for example, grandparent to grandchild is a generation distance of two.

questions.question: What is a 'two-side family tree' used to represent?
options: A family tree with two roots to model marriage between two separate families
A tree with only two people
A tree that can only have two generations
A tree with two identical copies of the same person
questions.rationale: A two-side family tree models a marriage as joining two separate family lines together, letting you trace relations both through the person's own side and their spouse's side.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a 'sibling' and a 'half-sibling'?
options: There is no difference
Full siblings share both parents; half-siblings share only one parent
Half-siblings are always older
Sibling only applies to sisters, half-sibling only to brothers
questions.rationale: Full siblings share both parents, while half-siblings share exactly one parent — a distinction that matters when a family graph includes a parent who has children from more than one relationship.

questions.question: What is a 'step relation' (e.g., step-mother, step-brother)?
options: A biological blood relation like any other
A relation created through a parent's remarriage, without a direct biological link to the step-relative
A relation that only exists in fiction, never in reasoning questions
Another term for cousin
questions.rationale: Step relations arise from a parent's remarriage — a step-mother, for instance, is a parent's spouse with no direct biological link, distinct from a biological ('blood') relation.

questions.question: What kind of link does a 'marriage / in-law' connection represent in a family graph?
options: A parent-child link
A link connecting two family lines through marriage rather than through birth
A sibling link
It isn't represented in a family graph at all
questions.rationale: Marriage/in-law links connect two otherwise-separate family lines through a spouse relationship, distinct from the birth-based parent-child and sibling links.

questions.question: What does 'relation normalization' mean when solving a complex blood relation problem?
options: Converting every relation term to its most basic, consistent form (e.g., resolving 'my father's brother' to 'uncle') to avoid ambiguity during composition
Deleting relations that seem unimportant
Only applies to spouse relations
Making every person the same gender for simplicity
questions.rationale: Normalization means converting varied phrasings of a relation into one consistent, unambiguous form before composing them, which prevents errors from treating equivalent phrasings as if they were different relations.

questions.question: Why is a relation table for quick inference useful when solving under time pressure?
options: It replaces the need to read the question at all
It lets you look up the result of a common composition (like 'mother's brother') instantly instead of re-deriving it from scratch each time
It only works for one specific question
It removes the need for a family graph entirely
questions.rationale: A quick-reference relation table lets you instantly recall the result of common relation compositions rather than re-deriving the same composition from first principles under time pressure.

questions.question: In a more complex example involving multiple statements, what is the recommended solving method?
options: Read all statements at once and guess the final relation
Build the family graph incrementally, statement by statement, checking for contradictions as each new link is added
Only use the last statement given
Ignore statements that mention marriage
questions.rationale: The recommended method builds the family graph incrementally as each statement is processed, checking each new link against what's already established rather than trying to absorb every statement at once.

questions.question: What is the purpose of tracking generation distance explicitly, rather than just relation names?
options: It has no practical benefit
It helps distinguish between similarly-named relations that differ only in generation, like 'uncle' vs 'grand-uncle'
It is only used for spouse relations
It replaces the need for gender tracking
questions.rationale: Explicitly tracking generation distance helps distinguish between relations that sound similar but differ in generation — for example, an uncle (one generation up, sibling of a parent) versus a grand-uncle (two generations up, sibling of a grandparent).
